name: Vera Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead carpenter for Pryce Builders, a family firm out in farming country. We put up barns, stables, machinery sheds, and do repairs on farmhouses, so one week I'm framing a timber stable and the next I'm replacing a rotten porch for a widow up a muddy lane. I like that the customers are neighbours, you see your work every time you drive past. What wears me out is the mud, the winter mornings, and the long drives between farms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work for and with, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Old Mr Pryce started it and his son Gareth runs it now. I've got three under me, and a young lad on an apprenticeship from the farming college, which I pushed for. At home there's my husband Tom, who milks on a dairy farm two miles down the road, and our two, Ruben's thirteen and Ana's ten. We've got the mortgage on our cottage and, being honest, less than a month's money saved, because rural building doesn't pay like town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Ruben set up a thing on my phone where I can say what timber I need and it writes the order to the yard for me. It saves me squinting at a screen at night. I didn't trust it at first, but Gareth uses it and it's been right, so I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, back to work. At work I'd say the phone thing's handy and that's all I need. After church I'd tell people they can stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means life goes on, and our life is fine, just tight. Farmers keep needing sheds and porches keep rotting. Money stays the worry it always was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep using the phone for timber orders. I'd keep at Gareth to take on a second apprentice, because there's work for one. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money stays the worry. What's the biggest pressure right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter, when farmers stop spending. Gareth cuts us to four days in January most years. A four-day week in January means Tom and I eat a lot of soup and say grace like we mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push for another apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nobody young round here learns this anymore, they all go to the city. If we don't train them, in ten years there's no one to fix a barn. Old Mr Pryce trained me when I was the only girl on any site in the county.

S0.say: I'd say that's that then and go back to work, since the phone tool is all I need. After church I'd tell people they can stop worrying.
S0.think: I think life goes on, which is fine but tight. Farmers keep needing sheds and porches keep rotting, and money stays the main worry.
S0.do: Keeps working and using her phone for timber orders. Presses her boss to take on a second apprentice.
S0.quote: A four-day week in January means Tom and I eat a lot of soup and say grace like we mean it.
S0.fieldNote: Vera has adopted a small AI tool because she saw it work for others first. The plateau leaves her calm; seasonal winter cuts are her real pressure. Training young people locally matters to her, shaped by her own start as the only woman on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, it always has, and you either learn or you get left. At church and at work I'd say the same: look after each other and keep working. I'm not one for posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry for Tom more than me. His farm's already talking about a milking robot, and that's one less job straight away. My work's different every day, so I think it'd take longer to touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the bigger firms near town try out, and once I knew it worked I'd learn it. I'd start putting a little aside each week, even if it's just twenty. I'd talk to Tom about what he'd do if the robot comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing about a farm sale you hope isn't the one next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the milking robot talk on Tom's farm.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farmer's son went to a show and came back with leaflets. It milks the cows when they walk in, no person needed. Tom said, well, it won't be cold at four in the morning, and then he didn't say anything for the rest of dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Tom to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's good with machines, he keeps that old tractor going with wire and prayer. I'd want him to ask to be the one who looks after the robot. Better to fix it than be replaced by it.

S1.say: I'd say change always comes and you either learn or get left. I'd tell people at church and work to look after each other and keep working.
S1.think: I think Tom is more at risk than me because his farm is already looking at a milking robot. My work varies every day, so it would take longer to touch.
S1.do: Waits to see what bigger firms near town adopt, then learns what works. Saves about twenty a week and talks with Tom about his options.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing of a farm sale and hoping it isn't next door.
S1.quote: Tom said, well, it won't be cold at four in the morning, and then he didn't say anything for the rest of dinner.
S1.fieldNote: Vera's worry moves straight to her husband's job, where automation is already being discussed. She plans to follow others once tools are proven, in line with her steady nature. Her advice to Tom is practical: be the one who fixes the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and families are going to pay for it. At church I'd say we need to stand by each other, because the government won't be quick enough. I wouldn't be one for shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's frightening. Tom's job and mine both gone in two years, less than a month's money, and the cottage still owing. There's nothing else round here, it's farms and us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, Tom and I would sit down and cut everything we could, the satellite TV, Ana's riding lessons, the holiday at my sister's. I'd take any repair job going on weekends, cash or swap. And I'd talk to my sister and Tom's parents about help if it came to it, because family's where you go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper knot-in-the-stomach scared, and praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you usually wait to see things work first. Can you do that with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the frightening part. I like to see Gareth try a thing before I do. With two years, by the time Gareth's tried it, it'll be the robot telling Gareth what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruben and Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, gently. Ruben's thirteen, he'd want to help, he'd probably offer his paper round money, bless him. I'd tell him to keep it and keep studying.

S2.say: I'd say it's come too fast and families will pay for it. At church I'd say we must stand by each other because government won't move quickly enough.
S2.think: I think it's frightening: both our jobs gone in two years, less than a month saved and the cottage still owing. There's nothing round here but farms and our firm.
S2.do: Cuts satellite TV, riding lessons and the family holiday in the first week. Takes weekend repair jobs for cash or swaps and asks her sister and in-laws for help if needed.
S2.feel: Scared, with a knot in her stomach, and praying a lot.
S2.quote: With two years, by the time Gareth's tried it, it'll be the robot telling Gareth what to do.
S2.fieldNote: Two years takes away Vera's habit of waiting for proof, and she says so. With both household jobs exposed, she turns to family and church before government. Her son offering his paper round money is a small, vivid detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, if people get on with it. I'd tell the lads to learn the new kit when it comes. At church I'd say teach your children a practical skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to see who gets it right first and follow them. Gareth would probably buy something, and I'd want to be the one who learns it. Tom has time to become the robot man on his farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every week, more than twenty if I can. Once Gareth brought in a robot, I'd learn to run it properly, and I'd push to go on whatever training the supplier offers. I'd make sure Tom put his name forward for the milking robot course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Like a long winter you can stock up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the robots would be able to do on your kind of jobs by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know, I'm not a computer person. Probably the big repeat work, putting up the same shed frame over and over. I can't picture a robot sweet-talking old Mrs Daley into letting it take her porch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be the one who learns it. Would Gareth choose you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure he did. I've been there nineteen years and I know every farm in the valley. If he picks the young lad, fine, but I'd go and ask before he decides.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get ready if people get on with it. I'd tell colleagues to learn the new kit and parents to teach children practical skills.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to watch who gets it right and follow them. I'd want to be the one who learns the robot at work, and Tom has time to become the robot man on his farm.
S3.do: Saves weekly and learns to run whatever robot her boss buys, including supplier training. Makes sure Tom applies for the milking robot course.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, like stocking up for a long winter.
S3.quote: I can't picture a robot sweet-talking old Mrs Daley into letting it take her porch off.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Vera's follow-the-proven approach, so her mood eases. She is honest that she can't picture what robots will do and falls back on customer relationships. She'd actively claim the new role rather than wait to be chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for a sensible family to plan. I'd say it at church and to the lads. Same as I'd say about any big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the easiest one by a mile. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and the cottage would be well on the way to paid. It still ends the same, but we'd have had time to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give it a few years to see which jobs last, then retrain into whatever's sturdiest, maybe managing the robots on farm buildings. I'd put money aside for the kids' training and make sure Ruben does a practical course alongside anything else. Keep going at Pryce's while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not much more than any other big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Ruben's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He loves animals like his dad, he wants to be a vet. I'd say good, and do the farm college too, so you can fix a gate as well as a cow. Brains get you the job, but it's your hands that get you through a bad winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this ten-year picture that you'd miss, even if you were fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trade itself. Driving past a barn I built and knowing it was me. If robots do all of it, nobody drives past and says that's Vera's barn.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for a sensible family to plan. I'd say it at church and to my crew like any other big change.
S4.think: I think ten years is by far the easiest, at fifty-three with grown kids and the cottage well on its way to paid off. It ends the same but we'd have time to change.
S4.do: Waits a few years to see which jobs last, then retrains into the sturdiest, maybe managing robots on farm buildings. Saves for her children's training and keeps working at Pryce's meanwhile.
S4.feel: Uneasy, about as much as any big change.
S4.quote: Brains get you the job, but it's your hands that get you through a bad winter.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Vera plan at her own careful pace. What she would miss is pride in work people can see, not just the wage. Her advice to her son mixes study with practical skills, in line with her views on apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes Tom and me together. What would help is apprenticeships and training for grown-ups out here, not just in the city, and a bit of breathing room from the bank while families get back on their feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask about the countryside. In town you lose your job and there's another shop down the road, but out here you lose your job and the next one's forty miles away.

headlineQuote: In town you lose your job and there's another shop down the road, but out here you lose your job and the next one's forty miles away.
portrait: Vera Lopez is a 43-year-old lead carpenter for a family firm building barns and repairing farmhouses, with two kids, a husband who milks on a dairy farm, a mortgage and less than a month saved. She uses a voice tool for timber orders now and then, after seeing her boss use it. Her faith, family and training young people matter a lot to her. She is calm about the plateau and uneasy about steady disruption, mainly for her husband's job. AGI in two years alarms her because it hits both incomes before she can see what works, while five and ten years let her follow proven steps and retrain.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take her job and her husband's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and adult training in rural areas, not only in cities, and breathing room from the bank while families recover.
